previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and coronary artery disease presented with fever and shortness of breath from dialysis. She was found to have culture-negative sepsis, a type 2 NSTEMI with rising troponins and EKG changes, and an acute GI bleed from a gastric polyp requiring epinephrine injection. She developed transient confusion likely due to uremia, which resolved after dialysis. An episode of asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia occurred, managed with IV amiodarone, though it was discontinued due to QTc prolongation. Calciphylaxis in her thighs was treated with wound care and intralesional sodium thiosulfate, while IV therapy was avoided due to arrhythmia risk. Antibiotics were adjusted based on clinical course and dialysis needs. She stabilized, completed treatment, and was discharged to extended care with optimized medications, including fentanyl for pain, cinacalcet, and avoidance of QT-prolonging and calciphylaxis-exacerbating agents.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear ___,

___ was a pleasure taking care of you at ___ 
___.

Why were you hospitalized?
==========================
You had an abnormal heart rhythm that was very fast during your 
dialysis session.

What happened while you were here?
==================================
- Your fast heart rate was treated with a medicine (Amiodarone) 
which stopped the abnormal rhythm.
- You were started on heart rhythm medications (Amiodarone and 
Mexilitine) to keep your heart from going into an abnormal 
rhythm.  These medications can cause other problems in your 
heart rhythm system, so you were closely monitored.
- The nephrology team followed you during your hospital stay; 
you got dialysis without complications and you had a fistulogram 
(which had previously been scheduled outpatient).
- You saw a dermatologist, a wound specialist, and palliative 
care, who helped us in the management of your calciphylaxis and 
wounds. 
- We increased your pain medications regimen and your pain was 
better controlled.
- We discussed the risks and benefits of the treatment of your 
skin lesions with intra-venous thiosulfate: this treatment might 
improve your skin lesions at an elevated risk of abnormal heart 
rhythm. You decided to discuss this issue with you health care 
proxy and communicate your decision with your nephrologist and 
dermatologist.

What should you do after you leave the hospital:
================================================
- Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.
- Follow up with all your doctor appointments.
- Continue to take all your medications as prescribed.
- Make sure to discuss the risks and benefits of the skin 
treatment with you health care proxy and communicate your 
decision with your nephrologist and dermatologist.
